# MOVEit Transfer / CL0P Mass Exploitation: Investigation Report

## Executive Summary

This report traces the exploitation of the MOVEit Transfer vulnerability CVE-2023-34362 from its public disclosure and initial exploitation through deployment of the LEMURLOOT web shell, attribution to FIN11, and subsequent public association with the CL0P extortion operation.

The evidence supports the following assessment: CVE-2023-34362 was a critical, unauthenticated SQL-injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application that was exploited in the wild before or around the time of public disclosure. Mandiant observed exploitation beginning no later than May 27, 2023, while Progress publicly announced the vulnerability on May 31. The vulnerability was assigned CVE-2023-34362 and published in the National Vulnerability Database on June 2. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

Following exploitation, actors deployed the LEMURLOOT ASP.NET web shell, commonly using filenames such as `human2.aspx` and `_human2.aspx` to resemble legitimate MOVEit components. LEMURLOOT enabled the actors to enumerate files and folders, obtain database and Azure Blob Storage configuration information, retrieve files, and create or delete a user named “Health Check Service.” These capabilities indicate that the operation was designed primarily for data theft and persistence or operational access within compromised MOVEit environments. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Mandiant initially tracked the activity as UNC4857 but updated its assessment on June 9, 2023, merging UNC4857 into FIN11 based on overlaps in targeting, infrastructure, certificates, and the CL0P data leak site. On June 6, the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site claimed responsibility and threatened victims with publication of stolen data unless an extortion fee was paid. The evidence therefore supports a FIN11 attribution assessment and a strong operational association with the CL0P-branded extortion infrastructure, while the data does not independently establish the legal identity or organizational structure of the operators behind the CL0P brand. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Sources and Method

Only two source records were provided:

| Source ID | Source | Principal evidentiary role |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Mandiant, “Zero-Day Vulnerability in MOVEit Transfer Exploited for Data Theft,” reproduced through the CISA advisory URL | Intrusion timeline, LEMURLOOT behavior, infrastructure, attribution, and CL0P extortion claims |
| S2 | National Vulnerability Database, CVE-2023-34362 detail page | Vulnerability description, severity, affected products, CISA KEV status, and patch-version records |

The CISA URL supplied in the evidence contains the Mandiant Google Cloud Blog content rather than a separately reproduced CISA-authored technical narrative. Accordingly, this report treats S1 as the Mandiant technical and attribution source represented by that URL and S2 as the NVD vulnerability record.

## Vulnerability and Disclosure Timeline

### Technical nature of CVE-2023-34362

CVE-2023-34362 was a SQL-injection vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer web application. According to the NVD record, an unauthenticated attacker could potentially access the MOVEit Transfer database, infer database structure and contents, and—depending on the database engine—execute SQL statements that altered or deleted database elements. The affected database technologies included MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, and Azure SQL. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

NVD assigned the vulnerability a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8, categorized as Critical, with the vector `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H`. In practical terms, the record describes a remotely exploitable vulnerability requiring no privileges or user interaction and capable of producing high impacts to confidentiality, integrity, and availability. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

### Chronology

| Date | Event | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| May 19–22, 2023 | Many second-stage hosts presented RDP certificates generated during this period | Mandiant assessed this as suggestive of infrastructure staging |
| May 27, 2023 | Earliest evidence of exploitation observed by Mandiant | Exploitation preceded public vendor announcement |
| May 28, 2023 | `human2.aspx` LEMURLOOT samples began appearing in VirusTotal | Indicates malware circulation shortly after observed exploitation |
| May 31, 2023 | Progress publicly announced the vulnerability | Public disclosure occurred after observed exploitation |
| June 2, 2023 | CVE-2023-34362 appeared in NVD; CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog | Government vulnerability tracking recognized active exploitation |
| June 6, 2023 | CL0P^_-LEAKS claimed responsibility and threatened publication of stolen data | Public extortion attribution claim |
| June 9, 2023 | Mandiant updated its reporting and merged UNC4857 into FIN11 | Attribution assessment based on multiple overlaps |

The sequence is consistent with a zero-day exploitation campaign: actors had already exploited vulnerable systems by May 27, while the vendor announcement occurred on May 31 and formal vulnerability-record publication followed on June 2. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a); [S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

## Exploitation and LEMURLOOT Deployment

### Initial exploitation path

Mandiant observed several POST requests to the legitimate `guestaccess.aspx` file before interaction with LEMURLOOT. This behavior was interpreted as evidence that SQL-injection attacks were directed at that file. The available evidence does not provide the complete exploit payload or a full request-by-request attack transcript, so the precise exploit syntax and every affected endpoint cannot be reconstructed from the supplied material. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

After exploitation, actors deployed LEMURLOOT, a C# ASP.NET web shell tailored specifically for MOVEit Transfer. The shell was written to masquerade as a legitimate MOVEit component. Observed filenames included `human2.aspx` and `_human2.aspx`, while the legitimate product contained a related `human.aspx` component. The masquerading strategy likely reduced the chance that a basic file review would identify the malicious file, although that explanation is an analytical inference rather than a directly documented actor statement. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Mandiant stated that data theft sometimes occurred within minutes of web-shell deployment. This compressed timeline indicates that exploitation and collection were operationally linked rather than representing a long-term compromise in every observed case. However, the source does not establish that every victim experienced data theft within minutes, and it explicitly describes the observation as applying to “some instances.” ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

### LEMURLOOT authentication and command structure

LEMURLOOT authenticated incoming requests through the `X-siLock-Comment` HTTP header and a hard-coded, sample-specific 36-character GUID-formatted value. Requests that failed authentication received an HTTP 404 response. Successful authentication produced an `X-siLock-Comment` response with the value `comment`. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The web shell processed commands through three HTTP headers:

- `X-siLock-Step1`
- `X-siLock-Step2`
- `X-siLock-Step3`

Returned data was gzip-compressed. The shell also connected to the SQL server using database settings retrieved from the MOVEit application through `SystemSettings.DatabaseSettings()`. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The principal functions documented by Mandiant were:

| Function | Observed behavior |
|---|---|
| Database and storage discovery | Retrieves MOVEit file, folder, owner, file-size, and institution information |
| Azure discovery | Retrieves Azure Blob Storage account, key, and container settings |
| File theft | Retrieves files by file and folder identifiers and returns them in compressed form |
| User creation | Creates a user with `LoginName` and `RealName` set to “Health Check Service” |
| User deletion | Deletes users matching the “Health Check Service” real name |
| Session insertion | Inserts the created account into an active MOVEit application session |

If `X-siLock-Step1` was set to `-1`, LEMURLOOT returned Azure configuration information and database-derived file metadata. If it was set to `-2`, the shell deleted the “Health Check Service” account. Other values caused the shell to process file and folder identifiers or create a user account. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

These functions support the conclusion that LEMURLOOT was not a generic web shell. It was purpose-built for MOVEit data discovery and collection, with additional functionality to create or remove an application-level account. The evidence does not establish whether the account was used for long-term persistence in every intrusion, because the same tooling could create and later delete it.

## Infrastructure and Operational Pattern

Mandiant reported that scanning and exploitation activity frequently originated from the `5.252.188.0/22` IP range. It also noted that interaction with the web shell and data theft came from different systems. This separation is significant because it indicates at least two operational layers: one used for scanning and exploitation and another used for post-exploitation interaction and collection. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Many hosts supporting second-stage operations exposed RDP on TCP port 3389 and used certificates generated between May 19 and May 22. Mandiant considered the certificate timing suggestive of staging activity. The evidence supports an infrastructure-staging assessment, but it does not prove that every system with a certificate in that period was operated by the same actor. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Mandiant also identified overlaps in Internet service providers, netblocks, and IP addresses between the MOVEit campaign and historical FIN11 activity. One IP address attempting to exploit CVE-2023-34362 had reportedly been used by FIN11 as early as January 2023. That system had hosted RDP and continued presenting the same X.509 certificate when the later MOVEit activity began. Mandiant used these overlaps, together with targeting and data-leak-site similarities, to support merging UNC4857 into FIN11. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Attribution and CL0P-Linked Extortion

### UNC4857 to FIN11

Mandiant initially attributed the MOVEit activity to UNC4857. In an update dated June 9, 2023, Mandiant stated that it had merged UNC4857 into FIN11 based on:

1. Targeting overlaps;
2. Infrastructure overlaps;
3. Certificate overlaps; and
4. Data leak site overlaps.

Mandiant further compared the campaign to prior FIN11-attributed data-theft extortion operations involving Accellion’s File Transfer Appliance and GoAnywhere MFT. These comparisons are relevant behavioral evidence, but they remain attribution analysis rather than independently verified proof of operator identity. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

### CL0P public claim and extortion infrastructure

On June 6, 2023, the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site claimed responsibility for the MOVEit activity and threatened to publish stolen data if victims did not pay an extortion fee. Mandiant also reported that Bleeping Computer had described a person affiliated with the CLOP ransomware group as claiming responsibility on June 5. The supplied evidence records these as public claims and reporting; it does not independently validate the identity of the speaker or prove that all activity associated with the CL0P name was controlled by one legal entity. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

Mandiant had not directly observed extortion emails sent to confirmed victims at the time of its report. It assessed that delayed extortion demands were plausible because FIN11 had previously waited weeks before contacting victims after exploiting file-transfer vulnerabilities. This is explicitly presented as a plausibility assessment, not a confirmed fact about every MOVEit victim. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore that the campaign was assessed by Mandiant as FIN11 activity and was publicly claimed through CL0P-branded extortion infrastructure. The available evidence does not justify stating as an absolute fact that “FIN11 equals CL0P,” nor does it establish that every CL0P claim necessarily originated from the same operational team.

## Affected Versions and Defensive Significance

The NVD record identifies multiple affected MOVEit Transfer branches and states that older unsupported versions, including versions before the explicitly listed branches, were affected. It also records affected MOVEit Cloud version ranges. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

The source material contains two different patch-version presentations. The original vulnerability description lists fixes such as 2021.0.6, 2021.1.4, 2022.0.4, 2022.1.5, and 2023.0.1. Later CPE records show updated thresholds including 2021.0.7, 2021.1.5, 2022.0.5, 2022.1.6, and 2023.0.2. Because the record reflects later modifications, administrators should rely on the vendor’s current remediation guidance rather than infer patch sufficiency from the earlier description alone. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

CISA added CVE-2023-34362 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on June 2, 2023, with a required action to apply vendor updates and a federal remediation due date of June 23, 2023. ([S2](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2023-34362))

## Findings

### Finding 1: Was CVE-2023-34362 exploited before public disclosure?

Yes. Mandiant reported earliest evidence of exploitation on May 27, 2023, while the vendor announcement occurred on May 31. The exact beginning of exploitation remains unknown. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

### Finding 2: What was the post-exploitation payload?

The principal payload was LEMURLOOT, a C# ASP.NET web shell tailored to MOVEit Transfer and disguised under filenames resembling legitimate components. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

### Finding 3: What was the operational objective?

The observed functionality and victim impact indicate large-scale data theft, including possible theft from Azure Blob Storage where MOVEit data was stored there. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

### Finding 4: Who did Mandiant assess as responsible?

Mandiant updated its attribution from UNC4857 to FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and data-leak-site overlaps. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

### Finding 5: How was CL0P involved?

The CL0P^_-LEAKS site publicly claimed responsibility and threatened extortion. This establishes a public CL0P-linked claim and extortion channel, but not independently proven organizational identity. ([S1](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-158a))

## Overall Assessment

The evidence supports a high-confidence reconstruction of a mass exploitation campaign in which a critical, remotely exploitable MOVEit Transfer SQL-injection vulnerability was used before or around public disclosure to deploy a purpose-built web shell and steal files. The campaign’s technical design—targeting `guestaccess.aspx`, deploying disguised ASP.NET shells, querying MOVEit databases, extracting Azure storage settings, and retrieving files—demonstrates a focused data-theft operation rather than opportunistic vulnerability scanning alone.

My assessment is that the most supportable attribution statement is: **Mandiant assessed the MOVEit exploitation campaign as FIN11 activity, and the operation was publicly connected to CL0P through the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site and related extortion claims.** The evidence is insufficient to state with certainty that FIN11 and CL0P are identical entities or that every actor using the CL0P brand participated in the technical exploitation.

This blog post has been updated to reflect the new attribution and supporting evidence. Mandiant has observed wide exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer secure managed file transfer software for subsequent data theft. This vulnerability was announced by Progress Software Corporation on May 31, 2023 and has been assigned CVE-2023-34362. Based on initial analysis from Mandiant incident response engagements, the earliest evidence of exploitation occurred on May 27, 2023 resulting in deployment of web shells and data theft. In some instances, data theft has occurred within minutes of the deployment of web shells. The seemingly opportunistic nature of this campaign and the subsequent data theft is consistent with activity we’ve seen from extortion actors; however, victims did not initially receive any ransom demands. Then on June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site (DLS) claimed responsibility for this activity and threatened to post stolen data if victims did not pay an extortion fee. Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and DLS overlaps. This campaign has impacted organizations operating in a wide range of industries based in Canada, India, and the U.S., but the impact is almost certainly broader than Mandiant has directly observed. Following exploitation of the vulnerability, the threat actors are deploying a newly discovered LEMURLOOT web shell with filenames that masquerade as human.aspx, which is a legitimate component of the MOVEit Transfer software. Mandiant has observed several POST requests made to the legitimate guestaccess.aspx file before interaction with the LEMURLOOT webshell, indicating SQL injection attacks were directed towards that file. We have observed LEMURLOOT samples with the filenames human2.aspx and _human2.aspx. Various samples with the name human2.aspx were uploaded to VirusTotal beginning on May 28, 2023. Samples of LEMURLOOT have been uploaded to public repositories from several additional countries—including Italy, Pakistan, and Germany—suggesting that UNC4857 has also impacted organizations in these nations. LEMURLOOT provides functionality tailored to execute on a system running MOVEit Transfer software, including the ability to generate commands to enumerate files and folders, retrieve configuration information, and create or delete a user with a hard-coded name. Initial analysis suggests that the LEMURLOOT web shell is being used to steal data previously uploaded by the users of individual MOVEit Transfer systems. Mandiant is aware of multiple cases where large volumes of files have been stolen from victims' MOVEit transfer systems. LEMURLOOT can also steal Azure Storage Blob information, including credentials, from the MOVEit Transfer application settings, suggesting that actors exploiting this vulnerability may be stealing files from Azure in cases where victims are storing appliance data in Azure Blob storage, although it is unclear if theft is limited to data stored in this way. In many cases, the scanning and exploitation leading to the delivery of LEMURLOOT was sourced from IP addresses in the range 5.252.188.0/22, however interaction with the web shell and data theft came from different systems. Many of the hosts used to support these second-stage operations hosted RDP services with certificates generated between May 19 and 22, which is suggestive of when this infrastructure may have been staged. Analysis of this intrusion activity is ongoing and will be reflected on the CAMP.23.037 page within Mandiant Advantage; we will also update this blog post if and when additional information becomes available. Along with this blog post, Mandiant has produced a detailed MOVEit Containment and Hardening guide to assist organizations with this event. The document contains guidance on the following key items: Containment Measures Application and Infrastructure Hardening Logging and Hunting Recommendations LEMURLOOT Analysis LEMURLOOT is a web shell written in C# tailored to interact with the MOVEit Transfer platform. The malware authenticates incoming connections via a hard-coded password and can run commands that will download files from the MOVEit Transfer system, extract its Azure system settings, retrieve detailed record information, create and insert a particular user, or delete this same user. Data returned to the system interacting with LEMURLOOT is gzip compressed. Authentication and Database Connection LEMURLOOT first checks if an incoming HTTP request contains the header field X-siLock-Comment and a corresponding 36-character GUID-formatted value, which varies across samples. It effectively uses this GUID as a password and returns an HTTP 404 status code to clients that do not pass the expected header field and value. If the correct password is passed to LEMURLOOT, it sends a header response X-siLock-Comment and value comment, indicating the connection is successful and can accept tasking. The malware connects to a SQL server from the executing host using the settings retrieved using SystemSettings.DatabaseSettings(). It then processes data received from the connecting client, parsing expected commands from the following HTTP header fields: X-siLock-Step1, X-siLock-Step2, and X-siLock-Step3. X-siLock-Step1 Command Sequence If the value of the header field X-siLock-Step1 is -1, LEMURLOOT retrieves and returns the Azure system settings from MOVEit Transfer, including the configured Azure Blog storage account, and its associated key and container (AzureBlobStorageAccount, AzureBlobKey, and AzureBlobContainer). It then performs SQL queries to retrieve files, file size, folders, file owners, and institution name data. The resulting data is gzip compressed and returned to the client interacting with LEMURLOOT. If the X-siLock-Step1 header field value is -2, it deletes a user account with the LoginName and RealName set to "Health Check Service" using the SQL command in Figure 1. Note that this user is inserted using the following functionality. Delete FROM users WHERE RealName='Health Check Service' Figure 1: MOVEit user deletion command X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 Command Sequence If the value of header field X-siLock-Step1 is neither -1 or -2, the malware parses the values from header fields X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 and stores them in variables named fileid and folderid, respectively. If the values of fileid and folderid are not null, the malware retrieves the file from the local MOVEit Transfer system with these same values, gzip compresses it, and returns it to the connecting client. If the fileid and folderid variables are null, LEMURLOOT attempts to identify an existing account with permission level “30” and InstID = the value set from "X-siLock-Step1" otherwise it creates a new account with a randomly generated username and with LoginName and RealName values set to "Health Check Service" This account is inserted it into an active MOVEit application session. Attribution Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and data leak site (DLS) overlaps. The activity is reminiscent of prior mass exploitation events targeting file transfer software and leading to FIN11-attributed data theft extortion via the CL0P^_- LEAKS data leak site (DLS). FIN11-attributed data theft extortion has occurred following exploitation of multiple other file transfer systems. From late 2020 to early 2021, threat actors exploited multiple zero-day vulnerabilities in Accellion's legacy File Transfer Appliance (FTA) to install the DEWMODE web shell. Similarly, in early 2023, threat actors exploited GoAnywhere Managed File Transfer (MFT) vulnerability CVE-2023-0669. Mandiant has identified numerous overlaps in the ISPs, netblocks, and IP addresses used in this campaign and historical FIN11 operations. Notably, an IP address that was attempting exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 was used by FIN11 as early as mid-January 2023. At the time this system was first used by FIN11 it was hosting an RDP service on TCP port 3389. This service was still active and presenting the same x509 certificate when UNC4857's use of the system began. On June 5, 2023, Bleeping Computer claimed that someone affiliated with the CLOP ransomware group stated that they were behind incidents in which the MOVEit transfer system vulnerability was exploited for data theft. On June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS claimed responsibility for this activity (Figure 2). Figure 2: CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS post Implications Mandiant routinely observes threat actors with varying motivations targeting sensitive data. For example, state-sponsored threat actors have demonstrated ongoing interest in targeting entities with policy research, military and government files, intellectual property, and personally identifiable information. Cyber criminals can also directly monetize stolen data via extortion operations, post it for sale on underground forums, or leverage it in secondary operations such as business email compromise. Mandiant has not yet directly observed any extortion emails sent to confirmed victims. However, in prior cases where FIN11 exploited vulnerabilities in secure file transfer systems, the threat actors did not send extortion emails demanding a payment in return for not publishing the data on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS until several weeks later. It is plausible that FIN11 delayed sending the ransom emails in an attempt to extend the amount of time that the zero-day vulnerabilities remained undetected and thus increase the number of victims and/or capacity to negotiate with a large number of victims simultaneously. Although the CLOP brand has posted to their DLS suggesting victims should initiate contact, if their TTPs remain consistent it is likely that the group will begin to initiate contact with some impacted organizations in the coming days and/or weeks. NOTE: this is exploited in the wild in May and June 2023; exploitation of unpatched systems can occur via HTTP or HTTPS. This blog post has been updated to reflect the new attribution and supporting evidence. Mandiant has observed wide exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability in the MOVEit Transfer secure managed file transfer software for subsequent data theft. This vulnerability was announced by Progress Software Corporation on May 31, 2023 and has been assigned CVE-2023-34362. Based on initial analysis from Mandiant incident response engagements, the earliest evidence of exploitation occurred on May 27, 2023 resulting in deployment of web shells and data theft. In some instances, data theft has occurred within minutes of the deployment of web shells. The seemingly opportunistic nature of this campaign and the subsequent data theft is consistent with activity we’ve seen from extortion actors; however, victims did not initially receive any ransom demands. Then on June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_-LEAKS data leak site (DLS) claimed responsibility for this activity and threatened to post stolen data if victims did not pay an extortion fee. Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and DLS overlaps. This campaign has impacted organizations operating in a wide range of industries based in Canada, India, and the U.S., but the impact is almost certainly broader than Mandiant has directly observed. Following exploitation of the vulnerability, the threat actors are deploying a newly discovered LEMURLOOT web shell with filenames that masquerade as human.aspx, which is a legitimate component of the MOVEit Transfer software. Mandiant has observed several POST requests made to the legitimate guestaccess.aspx file before interaction with the LEMURLOOT webshell, indicating SQL injection attacks were directed towards that file. We have observed LEMURLOOT samples with the filenames human2.aspx and _human2.aspx. Various samples with the name human2.aspx were uploaded to VirusTotal beginning on May 28, 2023. Samples of LEMURLOOT have been uploaded to public repositories from several additional countries—including Italy, Pakistan, and Germany—suggesting that UNC4857 has also impacted organizations in these nations. LEMURLOOT provides functionality tailored to execute on a system running MOVEit Transfer software, including the ability to generate commands to enumerate files and folders, retrieve configuration information, and create or delete a user with a hard-coded name. Initial analysis suggests that the LEMURLOOT web shell is being used to steal data previously uploaded by the users of individual MOVEit Transfer systems. Mandiant is aware of multiple cases where large volumes of files have been stolen from victims' MOVEit transfer systems. LEMURLOOT can also steal Azure Storage Blob information, including credentials, from the MOVEit Transfer application settings, suggesting that actors exploiting this vulnerability may be stealing files from Azure in cases where victims are storing appliance data in Azure Blob storage, although it is unclear if theft is limited to data stored in this way. In many cases, the scanning and exploitation leading to the delivery of LEMURLOOT was sourced from IP addresses in the range 5.252.188.0/22, however interaction with the web shell and data theft came from different systems. Many of the hosts used to support these second-stage operations hosted RDP services with certificates generated between May 19 and 22, which is suggestive of when this infrastructure may have been staged. Analysis of this intrusion activity is ongoing and will be reflected on the CAMP.23.037 page within Mandiant Advantage; we will also update this blog post if and when additional information becomes available. Along with this blog post, Mandiant has produced a detailed MOVEit Containment and Hardening guide to assist organizations with this event. The document contains guidance on the following key items: Containment Measures Application and Infrastructure Hardening Logging and Hunting Recommendations LEMURLOOT Analysis LEMURLOOT is a web shell written in C# tailored to interact with the MOVEit Transfer platform. The malware authenticates incoming connections via a hard-coded password and can run commands that will download files from the MOVEit Transfer system, extract its Azure system settings, retrieve detailed record information, create and insert a particular user, or delete this same user. Data returned to the system interacting with LEMURLOOT is gzip compressed. Authentication and Database Connection LEMURLOOT first checks if an incoming HTTP request contains the header field X-siLock-Comment and a corresponding 36-character GUID-formatted value, which varies across samples. It effectively uses this GUID as a password and returns an HTTP 404 status code to clients that do not pass the expected header field and value. If the correct password is passed to LEMURLOOT, it sends a header response X-siLock-Comment and value comment, indicating the connection is successful and can accept tasking. The malware connects to a SQL server from the executing host using the settings retrieved using SystemSettings.DatabaseSettings(). It then processes data received from the connecting client, parsing expected commands from the following HTTP header fields: X-siLock-Step1, X-siLock-Step2, and X-siLock-Step3. X-siLock-Step1 Command Sequence If the value of the header field X-siLock-Step1 is -1, LEMURLOOT retrieves and returns the Azure system settings from MOVEit Transfer, including the configured Azure Blog storage account, and its associated key and container (AzureBlobStorageAccount, AzureBlobKey, and AzureBlobContainer). It then performs SQL queries to retrieve files, file size, folders, file owners, and institution name data. The resulting data is gzip compressed and returned to the client interacting with LEMURLOOT. If the X-siLock-Step1 header field value is -2, it deletes a user account with the LoginName and RealName set to "Health Check Service" using the SQL command in Figure 1. Note that this user is inserted using the following functionality. Delete FROM users WHERE RealName='Health Check Service' Figure 1: MOVEit user deletion command X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 Command Sequence If the value of header field X-siLock-Step1 is neither -1 or -2, the malware parses the values from header fields X-siLock-Step2 and X-siLock-Step3 and stores them in variables named fileid and folderid, respectively. If the values of fileid and folderid are not null, the malware retrieves the file from the local MOVEit Transfer system with these same values, gzip compresses it, and returns it to the connecting client. If the fileid and folderid variables are null, LEMURLOOT attempts to identify an existing account with permission level “30” and InstID = the value set from "X-siLock-Step1" otherwise it creates a new account with a randomly generated username and with LoginName and RealName values set to "Health Check Service" This account is inserted it into an active MOVEit application session. Attribution Mandiant initially attributed this activity to UNC4857, which has now been merged into FIN11 based on targeting, infrastructure, certificate, and data leak site (DLS) overlaps. The activity is reminiscent of prior mass exploitation events targeting file transfer software and leading to FIN11-attributed data theft extortion via the CL0P^_- LEAKS data leak site (DLS). FIN11-attributed data theft extortion has occurred following exploitation of multiple other file transfer systems. From late 2020 to early 2021, threat actors exploited multiple zero-day vulnerabilities in Accellion's legacy File Transfer Appliance (FTA) to install the DEWMODE web shell. Similarly, in early 2023, threat actors exploited GoAnywhere Managed File Transfer (MFT) vulnerability CVE-2023-0669. Mandiant has identified numerous overlaps in the ISPs, netblocks, and IP addresses used in this campaign and historical FIN11 operations. Notably, an IP address that was attempting exploitation of CVE-2023-34362 was used by FIN11 as early as mid-January 2023. At the time this system was first used by FIN11 it was hosting an RDP service on TCP port 3389. This service was still active and presenting the same x509 certificate when UNC4857's use of the system began. On June 5, 2023, Bleeping Computer claimed that someone affiliated with the CLOP ransomware group stated that they were behind incidents in which the MOVEit transfer system vulnerability was exploited for data theft. On June 6, 2023, a post on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS claimed responsibility for this activity (Figure 2). Figure 2: CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS post Implications Mandiant routinely observes threat actors with varying motivations targeting sensitive data. For example, state-sponsored threat actors have demonstrated ongoing interest in targeting entities with policy research, military and government files, intellectual property, and personally identifiable information. Cyber criminals can also directly monetize stolen data via extortion operations, post it for sale on underground forums, or leverage it in secondary operations such as business email compromise. Mandiant has not yet directly observed any extortion emails sent to confirmed victims. However, in prior cases where FIN11 exploited vulnerabilities in secure file transfer systems, the threat actors did not send extortion emails demanding a payment in return for not publishing the data on the CL0P^_- LEAKS DLS until several weeks later. It is plausible that FIN11 delayed sending the ransom emails in an attempt to extend the amount of time that the zero-day vulnerabilities remained undetected and thus increase the number of victims and/or capacity to negotiate with a large number of victims simultaneously. Although the CLOP brand has posted to their DLS suggesting victims should initiate contact, if their TTPs remain consistent it is likely that the group will begin to initiate contact with some impacted organizations in the coming days and/or weeks.
